title: Distance, timing, angles, and structure
note: Fighting is managed at ranges: kicking, punching, clinch, and ground. Whoever controls distance and timing decides where the exchange happens. Stepping off the line of attack beats retreating straight back, and aligned joints with relaxed muscles until impact make strikes fast and solid.

read.title: Owning the space between you
text: Two fighters always share a distance, and that distance decides what is possible. Japanese arts call it maai. At long range only kicks reach; a little closer, punches; closer still, the clinch, where fighters hold, knee, and elbow; finally the ground. Bruce Lee summed this up as four ranges: kicking, punching, trapping, and grappling.

The fighter who controls distance chooses the exchange. A long-armed boxer wants to stay where the jab lands and the opponent's punches fall short. A wrestler wants to close in. Feints, changes of rhythm, and good timing let each one steer the other into the wrong range.

Angles matter as much as distance. Retreating straight back keeps you on the line of attack, so a determined opponent simply follows. A pivot or a sidestep takes you off that line while keeping you close enough to counter, ideally at the moment the attacker is committed.

Finally, strikes need structure and relaxation. Aligned joints let force pass into the target instead of collapsing, while loose muscles move faster because they are not braking themselves. Skilled strikers stay relaxed until impact, tighten briefly, then relax again.

q.q: Why is retreating straight back often a poor defense?
o: It keeps you on the line of attack
It removes you from every range

Why do skilled strikers stay loose until impact?
o: Loose muscles hit with less force
